"falling tone" is not a phonological category in Idakho ... [p. 6] ... Idakho is a conservative variety of Luhya, contrasting between underlyingly /H/ and /Ø/ classes of verbal roots. The present work identifies 8 distinct patterns ... distinguished by the number and position of melodic Hs within the macrostem, the tonal properties of verbal affixes,…

5220.idn: Idakho variety of Luhya (ISO ida, JE411); Ebarb's two primary consultants grew up in Malinya Sub-Location, Shirumba Location, Kakamega District, Kenya. Corroborating source (Paster & Kim 2011) describes Tiriki (consultant from Hamisi).
5220.tone: Ebarb 2014 (Idakho, first-hand, 556 pp.): TBU = mora; surface H vs L, moras may be underlyingly toneless; 'falling tone' not a phonological category; conservative Luyia system with /H/ vs /Ø/ verb roots, Plateau, Meeussen's Rule, melodic Hs; the word 'stress' never occurs in the body text (only in two bibliography titles) and 'accent' only names the acute H diacritic. Paster & Kim 2011 p. 78 (Tiriki, first-hand): 'the tone-bearing unit (TBU) is the mora... Tiriki has a three-way underlying contrast between H, toneless, and L that reduces to a two-way surface contrast between H and L (plus downstepped H)'; Meeussen's Rule, H Tone Anticipation, default L; nothing on stress. Nandama 2022 (Lwisukha noun tone, UoN MA): H, L, downstepped H and toneless syllables, 39 isolation noun tone patterns; p. 29 lists stress among suprasegments generically but never describes it; p. 2 'one can classify dialects by investigating tone and stress' is a general methodological remark. Hyman 2013 App. 3 lists Tiriki JE413 under 'positionally restricted vowel length', not among penultimate-lengthening languages. No source asserts or denies word stress; none gives a stress position.

tn.quote: The tone bearing unit in Idakho is the mora. At surface representation, the mora may bear either a high tone (henceforth, H) or a low tone (henceforth L); at underlying and intermediate representations, moras may also be unspecified for tone. ... e.g. [ée] rather than [êː]. This is desirable because "falling tone" is not a phonological category in Idakho, as the circumflex would imply. In addition, is simplifies representations of intrasyllabic downstep, e.g. [éꜜé]. Toneless moras and moras associated with L are unmarked.

5222.tone: Source describes a lexical tone system: three level tones (High, Mid, Low) plus six rising/falling glide tones, tone-marked on every wordlist entry; homorganic nasal prefixes 'with a very few exceptions... not tonebearing'. No stress rule exists in the accessible literature; coded tonal on the tone statement alone, as for the sister language Kuturmi (kutu1262).

5223.dq: Kaska, an Athabaskan language spoken in the Yukon and northern British Columbia, has phonemic high tones. [No sentence in any of the three sources locates a word-level stress; Moore & Tuttle describe only lexical tone plus phrase-level declination and phrase-final vowel lengthening.]
5223.prule: No word-stress rule is stated in any reachable first-hand description of Kaska. The language is described as having lexical (phonemic) high tone: short vowels and syllabic n are high or low, long vowels low, high, rising or falling (Moore & Tuttle 2003; Meek 2001: 105 'Kaska is also a tonal language'; YNLC alphabet: 'two basic tones in Kaska, high and low', contours = sequences on long vowels). Intonation: F0 declination, no final lowering, significant phrase-final vowel lengthening.
5223.quote: Kaska, an Athabaskan language spoken in the Yukon and northern British Columbia, has phonemic high tones. Short vowels and syllabic n can have either high or low tones phonetically, and long vowels can have low, high, rising, or falling tones. ... [p. 5] In this study Kaska was found to have declination of fundamental frequency, but no final lowering ... Kaska was, however, found to have phrase-final vowel lengthening ... [Meek 2001: 105] Note: [ɛ] and [ɪ] in unstressed positions are not contrastive or predictable. Vowel length may be phonemic, due to stress, morphological merging, or a combi…
5223.loc: Moore & Tuttle 2003 handout p. 1, section I, opening paragraph, and p. 5, section V 'Summary' (both read); Meek 2001 p. 105, note and text under Table 4.1b (read); YNLC 1988-90 'The Kaska Alphabet' booklet p. 9 = compilation p. 199.
5223.tone: Marked-high tone language (Athabaskanist 'high-marking'): Moore & Tuttle 2003 'has phonemic high tones', 220 of 308 text syllables unmarked (low), 75 high, a few falling; YNLC 1988-90 p. 9: 'There are two basic tones in Kaska, high and low. Low tone is not marked, and high tone is marked with an acute accent. The contour tones arise from a combination of a low tone vowel followed by a high tone vowel (rising) or a high tone vowel followed by a low tone vowel (falling).' On stress: Meek 2001: 105 presupposes stressed vs unstressed positions ('[ɛ] and [ɪ] in unstressed positions are not contrastive or predictable'; 'Vowel length may be phonemic, due to stress, morphological merging, or a combination of these') but never says where stress falls; Moore & Tuttle and the YNLC materials never mention stress. Morice's 1899/1904 'accent' statements catalogued under Kaska describe Tahltan (Western Nah'ane) and are excluded here.

5224.dq: The preferred stress pattern, for a word (and foot), is iambic or anapestic.
5224.heavy: not applicable (the root syllable is called 'heavy' and prefixes 'light', but stress is assigned by root vs prefix status, not by a weight computation)
5224.prule: Stress is predictable from morphological structure: only root syllables bear stress; the one or two reduced-vowel prefix syllables (lexical and productive prefixes alike) never do, so the word/foot is iambic or anapestic (prefix(es) + stressed root); suffixes that are not stems in their own right are unstressed and often absorbed into the stressed root syllable. Stated for 'Tangkhul languages' as a group from the author's own Standard Tangkhul (Ukhrul), Kachai and Huishu data; Khangoi is placed in the group by classification (p. 5, Fig. 3 'Southern' branch) and its McCulloch 1859 forms are retranscribed with the prefixal vowel symbol @ (e.g. k@na 'ear', k@tha 'new', P@mit, ch@t-lo 'weep'), but no Khangoi-specific stress observation exists in any source.
5224.quote: [pp. 11-12] In Tangkhul languages, stress is always predictable. Only roots bear stress, and prefixes never bear stress. The preferred stress pattern, for a word (and foot), is iambic or anapestic. That is to say, a stem usually consists of a stressed (heavy syllable) root and one or two unstressed (light syllable) prefixes. Suffixes that are not a stem in their own right are not stressed, but these often form part of the same stressed syllable as the root. ... [p. 5, on Khangoi] Nevertheless, it meets most of the criteria established here for classification as a Tangkhul language (see sectio…
5224.loc: sec. 3.1 'Prefixes and Stress', pp. 11-12 (pp. 11-12; page break after 'unstressed (light syllable)'); supporting: sec. 3 p. 11 item 1 ('They do not bear stress, unlike root syllables'); Khangoi paragraph sec. 1.1.1 p. 5 and Fig. 3 p. 5 (Khangoi under 'Southern' > 'South-Central'); data sources sec. 1.2.1 p. 9 (Khangoi data = McCulloch 1859, Grierson 1903, 'none of which record certain phonetic niceties such as tone'); transcription sec. 1.2.2 p. 9 ('5' = stressed root allophone of /@/, '@' = prefixal-syllable vowel).
5224.idn: Khangoi (Southern Tangkhul Naga), under the source's group statement for 'Tangkhul languages'
5224.exq_: In Tangkhul languages, stress is always predictable. Only roots bear stress, and prefixes never bear stress.
5224.tone: Tangkhul languages are tonal: root syllables carry lexical tone (high, low, falling; Kachai also low-mid); 'The unstressed prefixes are very short and cannot bear the full range of tonal contrasts observed in the stressed root syllables'; prefix tone is predictable on verbs and possibly contrastive in numerals and nouns (sec. 3.2 p. 12). The 19th-century Khangoi data record no tone (sec. 1.2.1 p. 9). Takhellambam 2014 (Descriptive grammar of Kabrang/Kaprang Tangkhul, Manipur Univ. PhD; assigned to khan1277 by Grambank, not by Glottolog or the thesis) describes two tones (level, falling) and says nothing about stress (a full-text search stress/accent/prominence/intonation over all chapters: 0 hits).

5226.prule: No fixed stress position. Stress (tekanan) is explicitly non-phonemic ('fonetis'); every disyllabic root cited (/anjiN/, /ambuN/, /rumput/, /induq/, /jonton/, /lambot/, /kumpal/, and with long vowels /bagan/, /baiq/, /hidup/, /haNot/, /jelen/, /buhuN/, /buluh/) is recorded in three free realisations: stress on the first syllable, on both syllables, or on the second (final) syllable. The variation is attributed to nada (loudness), which depends on speaker-addressee distance and emotional state and 'strongly influences' stress and vowel length. Only open juncture is treated as phonemic (2.2.2).
5226.srule: None stated; the 'both syllables stressed' variant ([ámbúN], [rÚmpÚt]) is one of three free realisations, not primary+secondary.

5227.dq: Rensch (1978) uses the term "stressed syllable" to refer to Full syllables. That term is appropriate in that Restricted syllables typically have lower intensity than Full syllables and vowel quality and tone contours are generally not carefully controlled. (p. 10; Full vs Restricted is a word-internal stem-vs-affix distinction; sentence-level focus is treated separately on p. 17.)
5227.prule: Stress falls on the stem syllable (Mugele's 'Full' syllable = Rensch's 1978 'stressed syllable'). Affixes, clitics and grammatical particles are Restricted (unstressed) syllables with reduced inventories; tense/aspect prefixes precede the stem and person/number suffixes/clitics follow it (e.g. r+ hwa:n -na 'I'll tell you', stem stressed, suffix unstressed), so the stressed syllable is located by morphology, not by counting from an edge. Stems are almost all monosyllabic; in the rare disyllabic stems the final stem syllable is the Full (stressed) one.
5227.srule: None described. Mugele (pp. 10-11, quoting Merrifield 1963:15) notes the ballistic/controlled contrast could alternatively have been called primary vs secondary stress but treats it as a syllable-type feature of stressed syllables, not a stress degree.

For polysyllabic words, lengthening coincides with the stressed vowel. 5231.heavy: McIntosh 1984:20 (as quoted): 'the last non-final CVC or CVV syllable' -- heavy = closed or long-vowelled syllable; Arnott's rule is quantity-insensitive.
5231.dflt: initial syllable (McIntosh 1984:20: 'the initial syllable of the nominal is stressed, regardless of its structure'); Arnott: initial in nearly all words anyway.
5231.prule: The two descriptions of nige1253 dialects, reachable only as verbatim quotations in Breedveld 1995 sec. 4.6.1, state incompatible rules. (i) Arnott 1965:78, Gombe: in nearly all words of more than one syllable the salient (stressed) syllable is the FIRST, with a few exceptions (some numerals, adverbs, question words, negative verb forms; Breedveld lists Arnott's non-initial examples cappand'e 'tens', jooweego'o 'six', teemerre 'thousand', ammaa 'but', korii 'hopefully', ndeye 'where', moye 'who', mi-noddataa 'I won't call'). (ii) McIntosh 1984:20, Kaceccereere: in nominals stress generally falls on the LAST NON-FINAL CVC or CVV syllable; if there is no such syllable the initial syllable is stressed regardless of structure (example 'kaceccere'en 'the people of Kaceccere', stress pushed back to the heavy syllable); for verbal complexes she declines to give a rule (1984:82: 'there is always one, or more than one, high-pitched syllable in the complex, which often does not sound stressed at all'). Breedveld (pp. 130-133) argues that Arnott (and Noye) 'wrongly equated high pitch with stress' and that the weight rule is correct: e.g. rawaandu 'dog' is initial-stressed for Arnott but penult (= last non-final heavy) for Klingenheben 1963 and Breedveld. Whether the disagreement is analytical or dialectal (Gombe vs Zaria) cannot be settled without the primaries.

"(C)VN syllables, which are considered heavier than (C)V syllables by J. Payne (1991:11) and Crowhurst & Michael (2005:56-57), do not change the regular stress pattern" (p. 84)... "in terms of vocalic quality, /a/-syllables are the heaviest and /i/-syllables the weakest" (p. 91, point 7).
5238.dflt: disyllables: 1st syllable; 3-4 syllables: 2nd syllable; 5-6 syllables: primary on 2nd, secondary on 4th; 7+ syllables: no regular iambic pattern (pp. 83, 86, 88-90)
5238.prule: Stress is non-phonemic and follows tendencies rather than rigid rules. Default (no bimoraic syllable): the final syllable is extrametrical and iambic disyllabic feet are built from the left, so disyllables are stressed on the 1st syllable and words of 3-6 syllables on the 2nd (= penult in 2-3-syllable words, antepenult in 4-syllable words). A bimoraic syllable (long vowel or diphthong) anywhere in the word is the strongest stress attractor and takes the primary (or at least a secondary) stress, even in disyllables and even word-finally (rowáe 'he eats us', róotaki 'that is', otháwinatakàe 'it has cursed us'). (C)VN syllables do NOT count as heavy (antaki, antami, antawo keep 2nd-syllable stress). Vowel quality acts as a weaker gradient: /a/-syllables attract stress (especially word-initially: hápokana, páminìro) and /i/-syllables repel it. In words of seven or more syllables the iambic pattern no longer operates regularly (author's summary, 2.5.4).
5238.srule: Penta- and hexasyllabic words with no bimoraic syllable: primary on the 2nd syllable, secondary on the 4th (okématzìri, ikántanàkiro). A bimoraic first syllable takes the primary and a secondary tends to fall on the 3rd (káakitàki, náakatàki); when a later bimoraic syllable takes the primary, the first foot gets a secondary (ròmaryáaka, nèwatyéero) - disyllabic feet tend not to stay unstressed. Word-final enclitics (demonstrative enclitics, conditional =rika, locative =ki, plural =paeni, exclamative =wee) and the possessive suffixes -ni/-ti tend to carry a secondary stress (fn. 35 p. 85; 2.5.4 point 6). The counter-expectative enclitic =maita carries its own primary stress (téemáita, káarimáita = two phonological words). The author states that the primary/secondary distinction is auditory and tentative (fn. 33, p. 81).

5239.tone: Theil 1992 (first and only full phonology of Nizaa; fieldwork Galim 1983-84) describes word prosody exclusively as tone: three distinctive levels H, M, B (M vs B subordinate to H vs non-H); nine lexical tones on monosyllabic nouns (H, M, B, HM, HB, MH, MB, BH, BHM) plus floating H (Ho, Mo, Bo classes, 10 lexical classes in table 5.3); downstep !H (rule 5.9); 'transport des tons' = shift of a syllable's final tone onto the following syllable (5.6); definite form of nouns = suffixed B tone (5.7); polysyllabic nouns carry any of the ten lexical tones on the FINAL syllable and only H, M, B, BH on non-final syllables (5.3, p. 47). Monosyllabic verbs contrast only H vs non-H. Nowhere does the article mention accent, stress or syllable prominence: no stress rule and no denial of stress. Kjelsvik 2002 (MA, sect. 2.1.5 'Tones') and Kjelsvik 2008 (PhD, 4.4.2 'Tones': 'a rich tonology, with three distinctive tonelevels and a number of tone combinations used as lexical tones... tones are regularily transported') likewise describe only tone and defer to this article; PHOIBLE 1317 lists H, M, L and contours.

(Schröder & Schröder 1984: 46 n. 3) -- the tonal statements are made over the word; no word- or phrase-level stress/prominence domain is described anywhere.
5242.prule: No word-stress rule is stated in any opened Toposa description (Schröder & Schröder 1984; H. Schröder 2002, 2004, 2013; M. C. Schröder 2004, 2026): the words 'stress' and 'accent' (as prominence) do not occur. Toposa is described as a tone language: high and low tones, a fall at the end of words and a rare word-final rise, a mid tone as a variant of H, raised H / lowered L from morphotonemics (Schröder 2002: 19); 'Tone in Toposa is grammatical rather than lexical. Tone patterns extending over phonological words mark case in nouns and tense in verbs' (M. C. Schröder 2004: 30). The only positional statement is tonal and hedged: on most verbs the high tone falls on the penultimate syllable of the word in non-past tense and on the final syllable in past tense, 'very tentative' (Schröder & Schröder 1984: 9, 46 n. 3).
5242.quote: [p. 9] In the past tense, high tone occurs on the final syllable rather than on the penultimate syllable as in non-past.³ ... [p. 46 n. 3] In most verbs the high tone seems predictable in so far as it falls on the penultimate syllable of the word in non-past tense. In past tense it falls on the final syllable. This description is very tentative yet and awaits further tonal analysis. For this reason high tone is only indicated when the contrast between past and non-past, is in focus. ... [M. Schröder 2004 OPSL 9 p. 30] Tone in Toposa is grammatical rather than lexical. Tone patterns extending …

5242.tone: Two-level tone system (H, L; word-final F and rare R; M as a variant of H) with grammatical function: tone patterns over the phonological word mark case on nouns (e.g. nominative pattern on nyaberu 'woman') and tense on verbs. Verb H tone is described as largely predictable by tense: penultimate syllable in non-past, final syllable in past (1984: 9, 46 n. 3, explicitly tentative; H 'marked with the acute accent' only where the past/non-past contrast is in focus). No source describes stress, accent or any non-tonal word prominence; M. C. Schröder 2004: 30 reports a rejected orthography proposal to mark tense with an acute on the verb's last syllable 'irrespective of the tone on that particular syllable'.

Due to morphotonemics, raised highs and lowered lows also occur ... [p. 53] Tense is marked by the tone pattern that extends over the entire verb and varies according to verb class, person, number, and tense.

qtr.text: On the stressing of words: in Pidgin the accent mostly rests on the first syllable, however long the word is (singsing, gáramut, sánguma = dance feast, slit drum, black magic). In the vernacular languages [Ak and Auwon] the stress in disyllabic words lies without exception on the first syllable, whereas in two-[sic; evidently three-] and polysyllabic words it shifts to the second syllable. With many-syllable words, however, a certain uncertainty could be observed in some cases, giving the impression that some individuals handled the accent rather arbitrarily.

dqtr.text: Proto-Ambon stressed all words of more than one syllable on the penult of the base word. Monosyllabic suffixes of whatever kind had no influence on the position of the stress. ... A fourth group has likewise moved the stress towards the end of the word, but only because a further monosyllabic suffix attached itself to the supporting vowel. 5245.dq: Das Ur-Ambon betonte alle mehr als einsilbigen Wörter auf der Pänultima des Grundwortes. ... Eine vierte Gruppe hat den Ton gleichfalls nach dem Wortende zu gerückt, jedoch nur, weil sich dem Stützvokal noch ein weiteres einsilbiges Suffix anheftete. Hierher gehören die Sprachen von Amahei, Nusalaut und Saparua.
5245.dloc: pp.174-175, sec. 177 'Die Betonung' (opening sentence) and a) 'Betonung und Stützvokal'
5245.prule: Amahei (Amahai) keeps inherited penultimate stress counted on the word including possessive enclitics (-u, -m, -ni) and the suffix -e (< -ke), which pull stress to the new penult (rimá-ni); the nominal article -ro/-lo and plural -ō are outside the stress domain (háu-ro, úsi-ro, lá'u-ō = surface antepenult), but stress never retreats beyond the antepenult: with two post-stem syllables (-o-lo, -i-ro, -ni-ro) it lands on the antepenult (husúr-o-lo, poó'-i-ro, hurú-nno).
